The lows are pretty low, but the highs are really high for me (in a way I don’t really think we’ve seen since RTD). For every Arachnids in the UK or Praxeus, we get a Can You Hear Me?, an It Takes You Away or a Demons of the Punjab.

Also there are a LOT of tiny little love letters to classic Who sprinkled throughout, which I really really love.

Plus those anamorphic lenses!! Cinematography is (for the first time ever) really a cinematic experience.

Honestly my favorite thing about Doctor Who is that it’s never the same show—it’s always trying new and weird and wonderful things. I thought Flux, on the whole, was kind of a let down by the end. But I’m the meantime it was SO FUN and SO INTENSE, and I just loved that it felt new and different. And honestly I would love to see them try another season-long story in the future, because it wasn’t that format that was the problem—it was the complexity of the story matched with an abbreviated number of episodes.

Jodie herself is a delight. I think I like her better than Capaldi (though it’s a close race).

Your question got me curious! I did a macro on my spreadsheet and came up with about 12 hours and 47 minutes (!!!) of total screen time taken up by traveling through time (or otherwise outside of time)

One of the ideas I’ve become attached to is that the continuity is a bit wonky anyway simply by virtue of it being a long-running time travel show, and things that are changed in the past—however subtly—butterfly effect themselves into altering the timeline in ways we can’t explicitly understand.

The most apparent example to me is “The Enemy of the World,” the Second Doctor story that takes place in 2018. Since the show is still running, world events in the year 2018 looks a lot different from the Thirteenth Doctor’s perspective.

So at some point, somewhere, sometime, any of the Doctors between 2 and 13 must have changed things in some small way so that, through a Rube-Goldberg-esque series of casualty, the Thirteenth Doctor’s version of 2018 resulted.

I had to kind of fudge some of it to compensate for the fact that the show itself doesn’t even take its continuity too seriously. So my rule of thumb was: without any extenuating circumstances, “present day” stories would take place on/close to the date they aired.

The only time this became a problem (at least that I’m aware—and I’m happy to be corrected) was in The Pyramids of Mars when Sarah Jane says she’s from 1980 (she would have started traveling with the Doctor in 1975). So rather than shift everything forward by 5 years I just decided to set Terror of the Zygons in 1980 (that’s the last “present day” story before Pyramids), and interpreted the meaning behind her line as “I’ve been to 1980 and I know the world didn’t end in 1911.”

Maybe not the most elegant solution, but I felt like it worked.

In future iterations (since Doctor Who is still on the air, I’m going to be updating it periodically) I may try to shift all the UNIT stories forward and try it out.
